❯ Write a 400-word paragraph about the history of tmux. Plain prose, no tools.

⏺ Tmux began in 2007 as a personal project by Nicholas Marriott, who wanted a terminal multiplexer that improved on GNU Screen, the tool
  most developers used at the time to keep several shell sessions running inside one terminal window. Screen had served well for years, but
  its codebase was old and its handling of modern terminal features, such as UTF-8 text and detailed terminal emulation, was awkward to
  extend. Marriott wrote tmux from scratch with a cleaner design and released it under the permissive ISC license, which made it easy for
  distributions and companies to adopt. The most important architectural choice was the client-server model. A tmux server runs in the
  background and owns the shell processes, while any number of clients can attach to it and detach again. This means a session survives a
  dropped SSH connection or a closed terminal window, and it can be reattached later from a different machine. Users could split a window
  into panes, organize work into named sessions and windows, and control everything through a command language that could also be scripted
  from the shell. Over the following years the project grew steadily through contributions from a community of developers, and the 1.x and
  2.x releases added better color support, mouse handling, and more flexible key bindings. Configuration moved to a plain text file,
  usually named .tmux.conf, which people shared in their dotfile repositories and blog posts, turning personal setups into a kind of
  informal culture. Plugin managers followed, letting users install community extensions for status bars, session saving, and themes. Later
  releases introduced features such as popup windows and more advanced layout tools, which kept the project relevant as developers'
  workflows moved toward remote servers, containers, and long-running build or deployment jobs. Today tmux is packaged in nearly every
  major Linux distribution and is available on macOS and the BSDs, and it remains one of the most widely used command-line tools for
  keeping terminal work organized and persistent.
